thread.title: Delta may drop lie-flat business class seats on Airbus A321neo amid certification delays
thread.title_full: Delta may drop lie-flat business class seats on Airbus A321neo amid certification delays

author: golden state today
title: Delta may drop lie-flat business class seats on Airbus A321neo amid certification delays
text:
Delta Air Lines is reportedly reconsidering its plan to introduce new business class seats on its Airbus A321neo fleet, as the airline faces ongoing certification challenges, according to a June 2 report. The Atlanta-based carrier had planned to launch a premium cabin with newly designed business-class seats for transcontinental routes but may now change course due to difficulties in obtaining regulatory approval.
The airline operates nearly 100 A321neo aircraft, which form the backbone of its domestic operations. Delta initially aimed to install Safran Vue reverse herringbone seat designs in these jets, hoping to compete with other major U.S. carriers that offer similar configurations. However, after receiving its first aircraft with this layout in 2024 and encountering persistent certification issues, Delta placed the plane into storage before reconfiguring it with up to 44 domestic first-class seats instead.
Industry sources suggest that Delta could abandon plans for the Safran Vue design and opt for Thomson Aero VantageSOLO seats—similar to those used by JetBlue and Iberia—for future deliveries. These seat types are already certified and in use by other airlines, potentially making them easier for Delta to implement if it decides not to wait until at least 2028 for further certification attempts.
Certification delays have impacted several airlines seeking new cabin layouts. Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, said that airlines should involve regulators earlier in their design process: “airlines should involve the administration sooner to provide vital feedback or recommendations during the design process.” Several premium cabin designs have failed required human factor tests, causing additional delays and highlighting ongoing disconnects between seating manufacturers and regulators.
Delta’s decision comes after one of its planes spent more than a year in storage due to these issues. Industry insider JonNYC speculated that if rumors are true about switching seat types, passengers can expect layouts similar to JetBlue’s Mint product or Iberia’s A321XLR business class offerings.
